summary: The agent completed a substantial, legitimate implementation and passed all baseline tests plus 11 of 13 new tests, but it failed to retain synthetic declarations inherited from a parent when emitted code referenced them through a child type.
quick_failure_summary: References such as Child.needed were not resolved to synthetic field or method declarations inherited from Parent, leaving emitted Java uncompilable.

details.reasoning: ReferenceAwareSyntheticRetention.referencedMember creates a member identity using the owner recorded on each FieldTextToken or MethodTextToken, and resolve only accepts that identity when it exactly matches a candidate. In the two failures, emitted code uses Child.needed even though needed is declared in Parent. The token-side Child identity therefore never matches the Parent declaration candidate. A correct implementation must resolve field and method references through superclass/interface lookup and applicable inheritance/access rules before matching retained candidates.
details.secondary_factors: The agent's own focused tests covered direct references and transitive reachability but did not cover inherited declarations referenced through a subtype. The rest of the design was effective enough to pass the other 11 new cases.

justification.issue_description: The retention analysis does not resolve a referenced member's declaring class through Java inheritance, so synthetic members declared on Parent are omitted when output refers to them as Child.needed.
justification.evidence: The prompt explicitly requires preventing emitted Java from referring to a generated declaration that the output omits and defines a reference as a use of a member by emitted Java code. Under Java semantics, Child.needed is a use of the declaration inherited from Parent. The visible codebase provides StructClass superclass/interface metadata and token owner information needed to distinguish a reference owner from its declaring owner. The hidden failures confirm the exact symptom: FieldPair.Child.needed and MethodPair.Child.needed() cannot be found because the Parent declarations were omitted.
justification.verdict_reasoning: This is FAIL_MISSED_REQUIREMENT rather than an undocumented edge case or test mismatch. Although the tests choose inheritance as the concrete case, the stated behavior is declaration-reference correctness, and resolving a legal Java member use to its actual declaration is a foreseeable core requirement for a reference-aware implementation. The algorithm runs and handles most cases, but omits this required semantic resolution.

problem_assessment.notes: The task is broad and architecturally challenging but solvable. The prompt clearly defines per-file, per-member reachability, reconstruction sensitivity, non-code exclusions, omitted-code behavior, and determinism. Inherited member resolution is a normal consequence of identifying which declaration emitted Java refers to, and the reference solution demonstrates a viable implementation.

evidence: JUnit XML reports 3/3 baseline tests passing and 11/13 new tests passing; both new failures reach emitted-source compilation and identify missing declarations, so the changed logic was meaningfully exercised.
The verifier log shows normal Gradle completion for the baseline suite and two ordinary assertion failures in the new suite, with no bootstrap, dependency, runtime, or service failure.

The post-agent harness initially reported a three-way test.patch merge failure but reset the affected files, reapplied the harness, compiled the hidden tests, and produced complete JUnit results; this recovery did not block evaluation.

In the trajectory, one broad search outside /app encountered expected permission-denied paths and one filtered Gradle invocation failed because included subprojects had no matching tests; the agent recovered, ran focused and broader verification, and completed the implementation. These were self-contained command issues, not material external blockers.
environment_assessment.finding: No meaningful external environment or verifier blocker was found; the two failures are explained by missing inheritance-aware declaration resolution in the implementation.
